newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentina's Fernandez hails "clear" IMF support.
newsitem.headline: Argentina's Fernandez hails "clear" IMF support.

text.p: Argentine Economy Minister Roque Fernandez said Monday the International Monetary Fund had expressed confidence that his fiscal package was the right way to narrow the budget deficit and return to growth.

He said IMF chief Michel Camdessus' support, expressed in a meeting with President Carlos Menem Sunday, "gave a clear message that the measures we have taken are sufficiently prudent to make the state solvent and maintain recovery."
After Camdessus' visit, Fernandez's aides expect a letter of intent with the IMF, outlining Argentina's revised economic goals, by Wednesday or Thursday at the latest.

Camdessus said he was "very confident" in the economic program, which includes a fiscal austerity package to try to slash a budget deficit that Fernandez warns would otherwise reach $6.6 billion by year-end.

The IMF managing director revealed a tentative agreement for another Extended Fund Facility "to complete the process of modernization in Argentina," starting in September 1997 and lasting until after Menem's current term ends in 1999.

Fernandez, the ex-Central Bank chief who replaced Domingo Cavallo as economy minister at the end of July, told local radio that the IMF's support showed that "sadly they see us better from abroad than we do ourselves."
Fernandez was put on the defensive in weekend interviews by criticisms from Cavallo that he exaggerated the budget deficit to "scare legislators" into passing his tax hikes.

He was also on the defensive against parting comments from economist Guillermo Calvo, who quit his economic team last Friday. Calvo told local radio this weekend that Argentina, which has had peso/dollar parity since 1991, needed a "real" or "indirect" devaluation, to help exporters by increasing non-Mercosur import tariffs and export subsidies.
Fernandez pointed out that Calvo proposed this solution "if the circumstances arise in which public spending and the deficit cannot be controlled -- which is not going to happen."
